title: Evaluating the capability of large language models to personalize science texts for diverse middle-school-age learners
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a large language model, GPT-4, can personalize educational science texts for middle-school students in a way that aligns with individual learning preferences. The motivation is to test whether generative AI can move beyond fixed, recommender-style tutoring systems and support more adaptive personalized learning in K-12 education.

The intervention used GPT-4 in two roles: first, to infer a student profile from choices made during a short training session, and second, to rewrite science passages to match that inferred profile. Students in the experimental group received texts aligned with their profile, while control-group students received texts rewritten to contradict it. The study involved 23 seventh- and eighth-grade students from one Connecticut middle school, who completed pairs of science-text choices on topics such as the water cycle, climate change, photosynthesis, states of matter, plate tectonics, and electricity.

Results from a Mann-Whitney U test showed that students in the experimental group were more likely to choose the personalized passages than those in the control group, with the difference significant at the .10 level. However, profile identification was only modest and not clearly above chance overall. The authors conclude that GPT-4 shows promise for personalizing science texts for middle-school learners, but the evidence is preliminary because the study was small, short, and limited to one school and introductory science content.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed randomized controlled trial with direct experimental comparison, but it is small (n=23) and relies on preference/selection outcomes rather than learning gains. The design is credible, but statistical inference is tentative given the marginal significance and limited generalizability.
impact_tier_rationale: The observed effect on paragraph preference is modest-to-moderate and limited to a narrow proxy outcome rather than achievement or inquiry performance. The sample is very small and the study does not show durable or broad educational impact.

interventions.use_case: GPT-4 used to profile middle-school students’ learning preferences from choice behavior and rewrite science texts to align with the inferred profile for personalized learning.

finding.finding_summary: In a small randomized controlled trial (n=23; 12 experimental, 11 control), students in the experimental group were more likely to select GPT-4 rewritten science paragraphs that matched their inferred learning profile than students in the control group who saw texts rewritten to contradict their profile. The difference was significant at the .10 level on a Mann-Whitney U test (U=40.5, one-sided p=.059); if analyzed as a t-test, the authors report a medium-to-large effect (g=0.715, t(21)=1.777, one-sided p=.045).
finding.measure: Preference/selection of personalized science paragraphs in a test session after profile-based rewriting

finding.finding_summary: The profile-evaluation task found that 14 of 23 students selected the true profile, which was not significantly different from chance (p=.405). This suggests participants were, on average, unable to reliably identify the profile GPT-4 inferred from their training choices, even though there was a group difference at the .10 level (Z=1.450, one-sided p=.074, h=0.615).
finding.measure: Accuracy in selecting the true versus opposite learning-profile description
